note: v0.25: methods from actuarial science, weather forecasting and big data, with how the engine could use each and the test that would show it helps.

methods.method: Buhlmann credibility shrinkage of strategy and forecaster edges
methods.what it does in its home field: Sets each policyholder's premium as a weighted average of its own claims history and the class average, with weight Z = n/(n+K) where K is within-risk noise over between-risk spread.
methods.formula: edge_i_cred = Z_i * edge_i + (1 - Z_i) * edge_pool; Z_i = n_i / (n_i + K); K = EPV_hat / VHM_hat; EPV_hat = mean over i of within-unit variance of monthly edge; VHM_hat = variance of unit means - EPV_hat / n (floored at 0)
methods.market analog: Each strategy, forecaster or regime model in the engine is a policyholder; its monthly excess return or forecast score is its claims record; the stable of all units tried is the class.
methods.how the engine could use it: Replace or sit beside the evidence gate's haircut: each month, compute EPV and VHM across every strategy ever tried (including dead ones), shrink each unit's mean edge and Sharpe toward the pool, and size only on the credibility-weighted edge. A VHM estimate of zero means the engine should treat all tried strategies as equally (un)skilled.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward on 1871 onward: at each month, rank units by raw trailing edge versus credibility edge and score next-36-month realized edge. Credibility helps if its out-of-sample mean squared error is lower than raw edge and lower than the pooled mean, as Efron and Morris found for batting averages, and if CRRA utility of the sized book rises.
methods.source_title: Dean, Topics in Credibility Theory (SOA STAM-23-18)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dean STAM-23-18 gives Z = n/(n+K), K = EPV/VHM and the nonparametric EPV and VHM estimators with VHM floored at zero; the VHM_hat form assumes equal n across units.

methods.method: Buhlmann-Straub credibility for regime-conditional returns
methods.what it does in its home field: Credibility for groups observed with unequal exposure, so a group with more exposure years gets more weight on its own average.
methods.formula: mu_r_cred = Z_r * Xbar_r + (1 - Z_r) * Xbar_all; Z_r = m_r / (m_r + K); m_r = months spent in regime r; Xbar_r = exposure-weighted mean return in regime r
methods.market analog: Regimes are risk classes, months in each regime are exposure; rare regimes (high inflation with falling CAPE, for example) have few months and should not get full weight on their sample mean.
methods.how the engine could use it: Feed regime-conditional expected returns and vols into the CRRA sizing step only after Buhlmann-Straub shrinkage toward the unconditional mean, so a regime seen for 40 months moves sizing far less than one seen for 400.
methods.test that would show it helps: Compare walk-forward forecast error of next-12-month real return using raw regime means versus credibility-weighted regime means. It helps if error falls most in rare regimes and the sizing path has fewer large reversals.
methods.source_title: buhlmannStraub: Buhlmann-Straub credibility model (actuaRE)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: actuaRE page fits Buhlmann-Straub with exposure weights and weighted cluster means; Z = m/(m+K) is the standard form.

methods.method: Limited fluctuation full-credibility standard as an evidence gate
methods.what it does in its home field: Says how many claims a risk needs before its own experience is fully trusted (1,082 claims for 90% probability of being within 5%), with square-root partial credit below that.
methods.formula: n0 = (y/k)^2, Phi(y) = (1+P)/2; for a mean with coefficient of variation CV, n_full = n0 * CV^2 (the chapter's severity standard applied to a mean); Z = min(1, sqrt(n / n_full))
methods.market analog: A strategy's mean monthly excess return with CV = sigma/mu; for an equity strategy with a monthly mean of 0.5% and sd of 4.5%, CV = 9, so n_full is about 1,082 * 81 months, far beyond any live record.
methods.how the engine could use it: Report for every rule or strategy the months of evidence it has, the months needed for full credibility at P = 90%, k = 5% (or a looser k such as 50%), and the implied Z. Cap the weight the evidence gate allows at that Z, which makes explicit that monthly equity edges are almost never fully credible.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward: apply Z-capped weights versus uncapped weights to strategies discovered in-sample and measure the drop in out-of-sample edge (the overfitting gap). It helps if the Z-capped book's live-minus-backtest gap is smaller and its deflated Sharpe higher.
methods.source_title: Mahler and Dean, Credibility (SOA STAM-22-18)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mahler and Dean give 1,082 claims (P = 90%, k = 5%), n0 = (y/k)^2, the severity standard n0*CV^2 (eq 2.3.2) and the square root rule (eq 2.6.3).

methods.method: Conditional EVT (McNeil-Frey) for the monthly expected shortfall budget
methods.what it does in its home field: Estimates one-day VaR and expected shortfall by filtering returns with GARCH, then fitting a generalized Pareto distribution to the tail of standardized residuals; it beat normal GARCH and unconditional EVT in backtests.
methods.formula: z_t = r_t / sigma_t; fit GPD to the k largest losses of z (k about 5 to 10% of sample, at least 50); z_q = z_(k+1) + (beta/xi) * [ ((n/k) * (1-q))^(-xi) - 1 ]; ES_q,t = mu_{t+1} + sigma_{t+1} * [ z_q / (1 - xi) + (beta - xi * z_(k+1)) / (1 - xi) ]
methods.market analog: Monthly real S&P returns since 1871 standardized by vol12 (or a monthly GARCH sigma); the GPD is fitted to the worst standardized months.
methods.how the engine could use it: Compute the book's next-month ES from the conditional EVT model instead of a normal or historical estimate, and size equity exposure so that ES at 97.5% stays within the 12% monthly budget. Exposure then falls automatically as vol12 rises, with a tail shape learned from 156 years.
methods.test that would show it helps: ES backtest (for example the Acerbi-Szekely Z2 test or exceedance count plus mean exceedance) on walk-forward monthly forecasts from 1900 on, versus normal, historical-simulation and unconditional GPD estimates. It helps if exceedance frequency is close to nominal and the mean loss given exceedance is matched, especially in 1929 to 1932, 1987 and 2008.
methods.source_title: McNeil and Frey, Estimation of tail-related risk measures for heteroscedastic financial time series (2000)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: McNeil and Frey: GARCH filter fitted by PML, GPD on residual tail, z_q formula and conditional ES match; ES of the residual equals (z_q + beta - xi z_(k+1))/(1-xi), consistent with the stated form; robust for k above about 50.

methods.method: Peaks over threshold with a mean excess diagnostic for crash and drawdown base rates
methods.what it does in its home field: Fits a generalized Pareto distribution to losses above a threshold chosen where the empirical mean excess plot turns linear, then reads off tail probabilities and return levels.
methods.formula: e_hat(u) = sum (x_i - u) * 1{x_i > u} / sum 1{x_i > u}; choose u where e_hat(u) is near-linear; P(X > x) = (N_u/n) * (1 + xi * (x - u) / beta)^(-1/xi)
methods.market analog: Monthly real losses and 12-month maximum drawdowns of US equities since 1871.
methods.how the engine could use it: Supply the regime models and the crash12 forecaster with a tail-based prior probability of a 15% fall, 25% fall and 40% fall, plus the expected further loss once a 10% loss has occurred (the mean excess). Use the GPD shape xi as a tracked state variable: a rising xi estimate on a rolling window is a tail-risk warning even when vol12 is calm.
methods.test that would show it helps: Stability test: estimate xi on 1871-1945 and on 1946-2026 and check overlap of confidence intervals. Predictive test: compare Brier score of crash12 forecasts using the GPD prior versus the empirical frequency prior in walk-forward.
methods.source_title: VGAM documentation: meplot, Mean Excess Plot
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: VGAM meplot page presents the mean excess plot as a GPD diagnostic with linear mean excess; the empirical mean excess and POT tail formula are correct.

methods.method: Return levels and the 1-in-200 standard as a risk report
methods.what it does in its home field: Insurers and hydrologists state risk as the loss exceeded once every N years; Solvency II fixes the capital standard at the 99.5% one-year VaR, a 1-in-200-year loss.
methods.formula: x_m = u + (sigma/xi) * [ (m * zeta_u)^xi - 1 ]; one-year 99.5% loss = 0.995 quantile of simulated 12-month book returns
methods.market analog: The 1-in-120-month (1-in-10-year) and 1-in-600-month (1-in-50-year) monthly loss of the model book at current sizing, and its one-year 99.5% loss.
methods.how the engine could use it: Add to each monthly decision a line that restates the ES budget as return levels: at this size, the book loses X% in a 1-in-10-year month and Y% in a 1-in-200-year year. Use the one-year 99.5% loss as a second constraint beside the 12% monthly ES so a string of moderate months cannot breach annual tolerance.
methods.test that would show it helps: Calibration: in walk-forward, the realized frequency of months beyond the estimated 1-in-120-month level should be near 1/120. It helps as a constraint if adding the one-year 99.5% cap reduces worst 12-month drawdown more than it reduces CRRA certainty-equivalent return.
methods.source_title: TU Delft MUDE, GPD: m Return Levels
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: TU Delft page gives x_m = th + (sigma/xi)[(m zeta)^xi - 1]; the 1-in-200 Solvency II part rests on Article 101, not on this page.

methods.method: Adjustment coefficient and Lundberg bound for drawdown-limit risk
methods.what it does in its home field: Ruin theory gives the probability that an insurer's surplus ever falls below zero; with light-tailed claims it is bounded by exp(-R u), where R solves the Lundberg equation.
methods.formula: For equity weight w and monthly excess log return r: solve E[exp(-R * w * r)] = 1 for R > 0 (exists when E[w r] > 0 and the loss tail has exponential moments); P(cumulative log return ever falls D below its starting level) <= exp(-R * D), the Lundberg bound for a random walk with positive drift (it applies afresh from each new peak, not to drawdown from the running peak over all time); under heavy tails replace with the integrated-tail asymptotic psi(D) ~ (1/theta) * B0_bar(D)
methods.market analog: The book's equity cushion above its drawdown limit is the surplus u = D; the expected excess return is the premium; losing months are claims.
methods.how the engine could use it: For each candidate equity weight, compute R from the empirical or GPD-fitted monthly return distribution and report the Lundberg bound on breaching, say, a 25% drawdown limit. Where R does not exist or the bound is far from the simulated ruin rate, flag that ruin is driven by single crash months and route the risk to an explicit tail hedge.
methods.test that would show it helps: Compare predicted breach probabilities with realized frequencies of 25% and 40% drawdowns by weight in 156 years of block-bootstrapped paths. The method helps if it ranks weights correctly and if the gap between Lundberg and heavy-tail estimates predicts where the normal-based sizing understated ruin.
methods.source_title: Koucha and dos Reis, Approximations to Ultimate Ruin Probabilities with a Wiener Process Perturbation (2021)
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page supports the Cramer-Lundberg model, net profit condition, Lundberg equation and psi(u) <= exp(-Ru); but the Lundberg bound covers falling D below the starting level, not drawdown from a running peak, which over an infinite horizon happens almost surely.

methods.method: Bornhuetter-Ferguson and Benktander updating of 12-month forecasts mid-horizon
methods.what it does in its home field: Estimates ultimate claims for immature accident years by keeping reported claims and taking the unreported part from a prior (BF), or blending BF with chain ladder using the share already reported as the weight (Benktander), which Mack found almost always beats both.
methods.formula: After k of 12 months, p_k = k/12 (or the share of 12-month variance elapsed); CL: ret12_hat = realized_k * 12/k; BF: ret12_hat = realized_k + (1 - p_k) * prior_ret12; Benktander: ret12_hat = realized_k + (1 - p_k) * [ p_k * CL_ultimate + (1 - p_k) * prior_ret12 ]
methods.market analog: A 12-month return forecast, an earnings-growth forecast, or a strategy's annual edge target that is partly realized; the prior is the engine's forecast at the start of the horizon.
methods.how the engine could use it: When the engine re-sizes monthly but scores forecasts over 12 months, update the expected remaining return with BF rather than extrapolating recent months, and use Benktander for earnings and macro inputs that arrive in stages.
methods.test that would show it helps: Over 1871 onward, at each month k = 1..11 within rolling 12-month windows, compare mean squared error of CL, BF and Benktander estimates of the final 12-month return and of 12-month real earnings growth. It helps if BF or Benktander beats CL at small k, as reserving theory predicts.
methods.source_title: Mack, Credible Claims Reserves: The Benktander Method, ASTIN Bulletin 30(2), 2000
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mack 2000 supports BF, Benktander as credibility mixture with c = p_k, and the almost-always-smaller-MSE finding; the Benktander formula is algebraically equal to realized + (1-p) * U_BF since p * CL_ultimate = realized.

methods.method: Claims development result test of the engine's own forecast revisions
methods.what it does in its home field: Measures the one-year change in the best estimate of ultimate claims; under a correct chain ladder model the expected change is zero, so persistent positive or negative development flags a biased reserving method.
methods.formula: CDR_t = F_t(target) - F_{t+1}(target); test E[CDR_t] = 0 and corr(CDR_t, CDR_{t-1}) = 0 for the engine's forecasts F of the same target (for example ret12 for a fixed window)
methods.market analog: Month-to-month revisions in the engine's own expected return, crash probability and vol forecasts for a fixed future window.
methods.how the engine could use it: Log every forecast with its target window, compute revisions monthly, and run a running t-test and autocorrelation test. Persistent one-sided revisions mean the forecaster is slow (underreaction) or overconfident, and the evidence gate should cut its weight.
methods.test that would show it helps: Inject known bias into a forecaster in simulation and confirm the CDR test detects it within a stated number of months; then on real walk-forward forecasts, check whether forecasters failing the test also have worse next-period scores.
methods.source_title: Merz and Wuthrich, Modelling the Claims Development Result for Solvency Purposes (2008)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Merz and Wuthrich define CDR as the difference of successive predictions with expected value zero under known CL factors; zero autocorrelation follows from the martingale property.

methods.method: Kaplan-Meier and hazard analysis of regime and drawdown durations
methods.what it does in its home field: Survival analysis estimates the distribution of time to death or failure with right-censored cases, and mortality laws describe whether hazard rises with age (Gompertz), stays constant (as found for public firms), or falls (Lindy).
methods.formula: S_hat(t) = product over t_i <= t of (1 - d_i / n_i); h_hat(t_i) = d_i / n_i; Greenwood: Var[S_hat(t)] = S_hat(t)^2 * sum d_i / (n_i * (n_i - d_i))
methods.market analog: Durations of bull regimes, bear regimes, high-vol spells, negative stock-bond correlation spells and drawdowns, with the current spell treated as right-censored.
methods.how the engine could use it: Estimate the hazard of exiting each regime as a function of its age. If hazard is flat, a constant-transition Markov regime model is adequate; if it rises with age (Gompertz-like), add regime age as a feature; if it falls (Lindy-like), lengthen expected persistence of mature regimes.
methods.test that would show it helps: Fit KM curves on 1871-1950 and test the hazard shape on 1951-2026 with a log-rank or Cox test of age dependence. It helps if a duration-dependent transition model has a better out-of-sample log score for regime changes than the constant-hazard Markov model.
methods.source_title: Kaplan-Meier estimator (Wikipedia)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia covers the product-limit estimator, right-censoring and Greenwood's variance; formulas are the standard ones; the constant-hazard and Gompertz remarks come from other entries.

methods.method: Excess-of-loss layer design and burn cost for the Treasury hedge
methods.what it does in its home field: Excess-of-loss reinsurance pays the part of each loss above an attachment (excess) point, capped at a limit: layer loss = min(max(loss - excess, 0), limit). Pricing from expected layer loss (burn cost) plus a load is standard practice but is not on this page.
methods.formula: layer payout L = min(max(X - a, 0), l) = max(X - a, 0) - max(X - a - l, 0); burn cost = integral_a^{a+l} P(X > x) dx, with P(X > x) from the fitted GPD; hedge efficiency = E[hedge payoff * 1{X > a}] / carry cost
methods.market analog: Monthly book losses between, say, 10% and 30%; the long-Treasury sleeve (or a put spread) is the layer; its carry versus equities is the premium.
methods.how the engine could use it: State the TLT hedge as a layer: estimate how much of book losses in the 10% to 30% band the Treasury sleeve has historically paid, conditional on the stock-bond correlation regime, and compare that recovery to the burn cost of the band under the GPD. Size the hedge only when recovery per unit of carry beats the burn cost per unit of carry.
methods.test that would show it helps: Over 1871 onward, measure the realized recovery ratio of long Treasuries in months with equity losses above 10%, split by corr36 sign, and compare the utility of a book that sizes the hedge by this layer rule against a fixed hedge and no hedge.
methods.source_title: Proteus Actuarial Library, Reinsurance Contracts (XoL.apply)
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: Proteus page supports the layer payout min(max(X - excess, 0), limit) but says nothing on burn cost or loading; home-field text trimmed to what the page supports. Burn cost formula is correct math.

methods.method: Four-module catastrophe model structure for stress tests
methods.what it does in its home field: Catastrophe models simulate a catalog of events (hazard), map them onto exposures and policy terms, apply damage functions (vulnerability), and aggregate financial losses into exceedance probability curves and average annual loss.
methods.formula: loss(event e) = sum over holdings h of w_h * V_h(intensity_e); EP(x) = P(loss > x) over the event catalog; AAL = mean annual loss
methods.market analog: Hazard: a catalog of historical and hypothetical shocks (1929, 1987, 2000 to 2002, 2008, 2020, an AI capex bust, a rate shock). Exposure: book weights in MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, META, NVDA, AVGO, TSLA, SPCX, ORCL and Treasuries. Vulnerability: per-name nonlinear loss given the shock. Financial: hedges and limits applied.
methods.how the engine could use it: Build the stress module in these four separable parts so each can be checked alone, and publish an EP curve of book loss with and without the Treasury hedge alongside the single ES number.
methods.test that would show it helps: For past stress months, compare realized book losses with the four-module estimate and with a single-beta estimate. It helps if the modular estimate has lower error, especially for the most convex names.
methods.source_title: NAIC, Catastrophe Models (Property)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NAIC page describes hazard catalog, exposure with policy terms, vulnerability damage, financial module, EP curves and AAL.

methods.method: Solvency II symmetric adjustment as a countercyclical risk budget
methods.what it does in its home field: Raises the standard equity capital charge when an equity index is above its weighted average level (36 months in the delegated rules) and lowers it when below, by at most 10 percentage points either way, a countercyclical capital rule.
methods.formula: SA_t = 0.5 * ((P_t - A36_t) / A36_t - 0.08), clipped to [-0.10, 0.10] (form as summarized by Milliman, Oct 21, 2024); engine mapping: ES_budget_t = 12% * (1 - SA_t)
methods.market analog: US equity price against its 36-month average; the engine's ES budget plays the role of the capital charge.
methods.how the engine could use it: Test a regulator-designed countercyclical tilt: shrink the 12% ES budget modestly after strong rallies above the 36-month average and expand it after falls, with the same caps, instead of letting realized vol alone drive size.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward from 1874 on, compare CRRA certainty-equivalent return, maximum drawdown and turnover of the base engine versus the engine with the symmetric adjustment overlay. It helps if utility rises without a material rise in drawdown; a failure would show that the regulator's tilt fights momentum.
methods.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 106 (EIOPA rulebook)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 106 supports the index-vs-weighted-average basis and the 10-point cap; the 36-month average and the 0.5*((CI-AI)/AI - 8%) form come from Delegated Regulation 2015/35 Art 172, not this page, and are correct.

methods.method: ORSA-style monthly self-assessment of model deviation
methods.what it does in its home field: Insurers must assess their overall solvency needs given their own risk profile, and how far that profile deviates from the assumptions behind the standard capital formula, as part of strategy.
methods.formula: deviation score = count or weighted sum of flags: realized vol12 vs model vol, realized corr36 vs assumed hedge correlation, realized tail exceedances vs nominal, forecast CDR bias, GPD xi drift
methods.market analog: The engine's assumptions (vol model, tail shape, stock-bond correlation, forecaster calibration) versus what the last 12 to 36 months show.
methods.how the engine could use it: Each month write a short own-risk assessment: which assumptions the book currently violates and by how much, with a rule that a deviation score above a set level cuts the ES budget or forces a model review before re-sizing.
methods.test that would show it helps: Backtest the deviation score as a predictor: months with high scores should precede larger ES exceedances and bigger forecast errors. It helps if conditioning size on the score lowers exceedance clustering without lowering long-run return much.
methods.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 45 (EIOPA rulebook)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 45 supports assessing overall solvency needs and deviation of the risk profile from SCR assumptions as part of strategy.

methods.method: EMOS (nonhomogeneous Gaussian regression) recalibration by minimum score
methods.what it does in its home field: Maps a raw ensemble to a calibrated Gaussian whose mean is a bias-corrected weighted average of members and whose variance is linear in the ensemble variance, with coefficients fit over a sliding window by minimizing mean CRPS. It turned a temperature ensemble whose nominal 66.7% range covered 28.7% of outcomes into intervals covering 68.6%.
methods.formula: y ~ N(a + b1 X1 + ... + bm Xm, c + d S^2); (a, b, c, d) = argmin mean CRPS over the training window
methods.market analog: The engine's monthly mixture-of-normals forecast plays the role of the raw ensemble: its mean m_t and variance v_t are the raw ensemble mean and spread, and the realized real return is the verifying observation.
methods.how the engine could use it: Add a recalibration layer after the forecaster: shift and scale each mixture component as mu_k' = a + b mu_k and sigma_k'^2 = c + d sigma_k^2 (c >= 0, d >= 0), fitting (a, b, c, d) each month on the trailing 120 months of walk-forward forecasts by maximizing the mean log score (the engine's own score) or, in short or crash-contaminated windows, by minimizing the closed-form mixture CRPS. The recalibrated mixture is what feeds the CRRA sizing and the 12% expected-shortfall check.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward from 1901: compare the mean monthly log score of recalibrated versus raw forecasts with a Diebold-Mariano test on the score differences (HAC errors); require a positive difference, a PIT histogram closer to flat (Kolmogorov-Smirnov or Berkowitz test), and coverage of the 90% interval within 2 points of 90%.
methods.source_title: Gneiting, Raftery, Westveld and Goldman, Calibrated probabilistic forecasting using EMOS and minimum CRPS estimation (MWR 2005)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: EMOS N(a + b1X1 + ... + bmXm, c + dS^2) fit by minimum CRPS over sliding (40-day) window, 28.7% to 68.6% coverage verified; formula correct.

methods.method: PIT histogram calibration check
methods.what it does in its home field: Evaluates each predictive CDF at the observed value; for ideal continuous forecasts these PIT values are uniform, and the histogram shape diagnoses too narrow (U shape), too wide (hump) or biased (slope) forecasts.
methods.formula: u_t = F_t(r_t) = sum_k w_k Phi((r_t - mu_k) / sigma_k); under calibration u_t ~ iid U(0,1) and z_t = Phi^-1(u_t) ~ iid N(0,1)
methods.market analog: The same transform applied to monthly real returns under the engine's mixture forecast; a 5% PIT tail is the frequency with which realized months fall below the forecast 5% quantile, which is a VaR exception rate.
methods.how the engine could use it: Store u_t for every month of the walk-forward record. Report a 10-bin PIT histogram, the share of u_t below 0.05 and above 0.95, and a Berkowitz likelihood-ratio test on z_t. Wire the left-tail exception rate into the expected-shortfall budget: if u_t < 0.05 occurs materially more than 5% of the time, the evidence gate widens the left tail before sizing.
methods.test that would show it helps: On 1871 to date, compute rolling 120-month PIT exception rates; months after a detected left-tail breach should show later breaches above 5% if the miscalibration persists, and a widening rule triggered by the check should raise the out-of-sample log score versus no rule.
methods.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PIT uniform for ideal continuous forecasts; U-shaped too narrow, hump too wide, triangle (slope) biased per paper; mixture CDF and inverse-normal z formula correct.

methods.method: Maximize sharpness subject to calibration as a model selection rule
methods.what it does in its home field: Orders forecast evaluation: first require statistical consistency between predictive distributions and outcomes, then prefer the forecasts that are most concentrated.
methods.formula: choose model j* = argmin_j mean predictive sd_j, among models with PIT uniformity p-value > 0.05 and 90% interval coverage within tolerance
methods.market analog: Competing return forecasters (valuation regression, regime model, analog ensemble, momentum model) each issue a monthly mixture; most are poorly calibrated in crashes.
methods.how the engine could use it: Have the evidence gate screen each strategy's walk-forward PIT record for calibration before ranking by sharpness or log score, so that an overconfident forecaster cannot win on a short lucky stretch. Report sharpness as the average 12-month predictive standard deviation next to the log score.
methods.test that would show it helps: Compare two selection rules walk forward: (a) pick the model with the best trailing log score, (b) pick the sharpest model that passes the PIT screen. Rule (b) should give equal or better next-period log score and fewer left-tail breaches, measured over 1901 to date with a block bootstrap.
methods.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper supports calibration first then sharpness; formula is a stated operational selection rule, internally coherent.

methods.method: Closed-form CRPS for a normal mixture as a second proper score
methods.what it does in its home field: Scores a Gaussian-mixture predictive distribution exactly, without sampling, using the expected absolute value of a normal variable; Grimit et al. present it for BMA predictive distributions, which are normal mixtures, while their own mesoscale ensemble verification uses the circular CRPS.
methods.formula: CRPS = sum_m w_m A(y - mu_m, s_m^2) - 0.5 sum_m sum_n w_m w_n A(mu_m - mu_n, s_m^2 + s_n^2); A(mu, s^2) = 2 s phi(mu/s) + mu (2 Phi(mu/s) - 1)
methods.market analog: The engine's monthly mixture of normals for real returns, scored against the realized return.
methods.how the engine could use it: Compute the mixture CRPS every month beside the log score. The log score punishes a tail miss without limit, so one crash month can dominate a comparison; the CRPS is in return units and more robust. Require a strategy to win on both scores before the evidence gate credits it, and report CRPS skill against climatology.
methods.test that would show it helps: For each pair of competing forecasters, run Diebold-Mariano tests on both log score and CRPS differences; count how often the log-score ranking flips when the three worst crash months are dropped, versus the CRPS ranking. A robust second score should flip less.
methods.source_title: Grimit, Gneiting, Berrocal and Johnson, The continuous ranked probability score for circular variables (UW Tech Report 493, 2006)
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: Formula matches Eq 5/6, but the paper gives the mixture CRPS as background for BMA mixtures; its own mesoscale verification uses the circular CRPS, not this formula.

methods.method: Skill scores against climatology and persistence
methods.what it does in its home field: Expresses forecast accuracy as the fraction of possible improvement achieved over a no-skill reference, usually climatology or persistence, so that a forecast is only credited for what the baseline cannot do.
methods.formula: SS = (S_f - S_ref) / (S_perfect - S_ref); for the log score use mean difference D = (1/T) sum_t [log f_t(r_t) - log c_t(r_t)] in nats per month; CRPSS = 1 - CRPS_f / CRPS_ref
methods.market analog: Climatology is the expanding-window unconditional distribution of monthly real returns known at each date (a normal or two-component mixture fit to all prior months); persistence is a forecast centred on the trailing 12-month return with the same spread.
methods.how the engine could use it: Publish D against both references in every report, with a block-bootstrap confidence interval, and make positive D against climatology a precondition for any non-neutral equity weight. Report skill by horizon to locate the skill horizon.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward 1901 to date: D versus climatology above zero with a 90% block-bootstrap interval excluding zero; D versus persistence also above zero. A strategy that fails either is flagged no-skill by the gate.
methods.source_title: WWRP/WGNE Joint Working Group on Forecast Verification Research: Forecast verification methods
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: JWGFVR gives the generic skill score with persistence and climatology references; SS, log-score difference and CRPSS = 1 - CRPS_f/CRPS_ref are correct.

methods.method: Murphy decomposition of the Brier score for crash probabilities
methods.what it does in its home field: Splits the Brier score of binary probability forecasts into reliability, resolution and uncertainty, separating fixable miscalibration from lack of discrimination.
methods.formula: BS = REL - RES + UNC = (1/N) sum_k n_k (p_k - obar_k)^2 - (1/N) sum_k n_k (obar_k - obar)^2 + obar (1 - obar)
methods.market analog: The probability of crash12 (a fall of 15% or more within 12 months) implied by the engine's forecast distribution, verified against the crash12 outcome.
methods.how the engine could use it: Derive p_t = P(crash12) from simulated 12-month paths of the mixture, bin into deciles, and report REL, RES and UNC. High REL triggers recalibration (isotonic or Platt) of the crash probability; RES near zero means the crash model carries no signal and should be dropped from sizing.
methods.test that would show it helps: Since 1871 with non-overlapping or HAC-adjusted samples: RES significantly above zero by block bootstrap, and Brier skill score versus the expanding base rate above zero. Note the small number of independent crash episodes, which makes BSS unstable.
methods.source_title: WWRP/WGNE Joint Working Group on Forecast Verification Research: Forecast verification methods
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Murphy 1973 REL - RES + UNC decomposition matches the page formula exactly.

methods.method: Cost-loss decision rule and relative economic value
methods.what it does in its home field: A user who can pay C to protect against loss L should act when the event probability exceeds C/L; relative value measures how much of the perfect forecast's saving over climatology a forecast delivers, plotted across C/L.
methods.formula: act if p_t > C/L; V = (E_clim - E_fcst) / (E_clim - E_perfect), E_clim = min(C, obar L), E_perfect = obar C; max V = H - F at C/L = obar
methods.market analog: C is the expected return given up by cutting equity exposure for a year (the equity premium forgone on the de-risked slice plus trading costs); L is the utility-weighted loss from staying exposed through a crash12 event, read from the engine's CRRA utility.
methods.how the engine could use it: Express the de-risking decision as a cost-loss rule on P(crash12): cut to the floor weight when p_t > C/L. Derive C/L from the CRRA risk aversion and the 12% ES budget rather than picking it, and report the value curve V(C/L) so the decision core can see which risk tolerances the forecast helps.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward from 1901, compute V at the engine's own C/L and across the range 0.05 to 0.6; value above zero at the engine's ratio and a value peak near the crash base rate. Compare V of the probability forecast with V of a binary signal (for example cape_pct > 0.9), which should be lower for most ratios.
methods.source_title: Richardson, Predictability and economic value (ECMWF)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Act when p > C/L, V definition with E_clim = min(C, obar L), E_perfect = obar C, and max V = H - F at C/L = obar all supported; formula correct.

methods.method: Ensemble Bayesian model averaging of forecasters
methods.what it does in its home field: Forms the predictive density as a weighted mixture of normal kernels around each bias-corrected ensemble member, with weights equal to posterior probabilities of being best over a 25-day window, estimated by EM. It brought nominal 66.7% interval coverage from 28.7% to 66.9% for temperature.
methods.formula: p(r | f_1..f_K) = sum_k w_k N(r; a_k + b_k f_k, sigma_k^2); E-step z_kt = w_k g_k(r_t) / sum_j w_j g_j(r_t); M-step w_k = mean_t z_kt
methods.market analog: Each forecaster in the engine (valuation, regime, momentum, analog) is an ensemble member issuing a monthly mean f_k and error variance; the realized real return verifies them.
methods.how the engine could use it: Combine forecasters with BMA instead of fixed weights: fit (a_k, b_k, w_k, sigma_k) by EM on a trailing window of walk-forward forecasts, producing directly the mixture of normals the engine scores. Shrink weights toward equal (a Dirichlet prior) because monthly windows are short, and let the evidence gate cap any weight earned on a short record.
methods.test that would show it helps: Out-of-sample log score of BMA versus equal-weight combination and versus the best single forecaster, Diebold-Mariano on monthly differences, 1901 to date; BMA should beat equal weights only if forecaster skill differs persistently, which is itself the test.
methods.source_title: Raftery, Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Polakowski, Using Bayesian model averaging to calibrate forecast ensembles (MWR 2005)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Posterior-probability weights, EM, 25-day window and 28.7 to 66.9 coverage verified; paper uses a common sigma, member-specific sigma_k is a valid generalization; EM steps correct.

methods.method: Spread-skill check
methods.what it does in its home field: In a perfect ensemble the time-mean spread about the ensemble mean equals the time-mean RMS error of the ensemble mean, and large-spread days should be large-error days; deviations reveal under or over dispersion.
methods.formula: ratio = sqrt(mean_t v_t) / sqrt(mean_t (r_t - m_t)^2), ideal 1; spread-error slope from regressing (r_t - m_t)^2 on v_t, ideal 1 with intercept 0
methods.market analog: The predictive variance v_t of the monthly mixture against the squared forecast error of its mean.
methods.how the engine could use it: Report the ratio overall and by regime and by vol12 tercile. A ratio below 1 in high-vol states means the engine is overconfident exactly when the ES budget binds; feed the regime-specific ratio into the variance multiplier of the EMOS layer.
methods.test that would show it helps: Since 1871: correlation of v_t with squared error positive and significant (HAC), and the regime-specific ratio closer to 1 after recalibration than before, with a log-score gain in the high-vol tercile.
methods.source_title: Palmer et al., Ensemble prediction: a pedagogical perspective (ECMWF Newsletter 106)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Perfect-EPS spread equals ensemble-mean RMS error verbatim; ratio and squared-error regression (slope 1, intercept 0 under calibration) are correct.

methods.method: Analog and constructed-analogue ensembles
methods.what it does in its home field: Forecasts by finding past states similar to today and using what followed them; because close natural analogues are very unlikely in high-dimensional systems, van den Dool builds a constructed analogue as a ridge-weighted combination of past states.
methods.formula: kernel analog: weights w_j proportional to exp(-d(x_now, x_j)^2 / (2 h^2)), predictive density = sum_j w_j N(r; y_j, s^2); constructed analogue: w = argmin ||x_now - sum_j w_j x_j||^2 + lambda ||w||^2, forecast = sum_j w_j y_j
methods.market analog: The state vector is the month's (cape_pct, y10, infl12, mom12_1, vol12, drawdown, corr36) known at the start of the month; outcomes y_j are each past month's ret12.
methods.how the engine could use it: Use the kernel analog as one more ensemble member that naturally produces a mixture of normals, with only months at least 12 months before the forecast date eligible to avoid overlap leakage. Use the constructed analogue as a point forecast for the 12-month mean. Keep the state vector short: Lorenz found too few close analogues even for weather, and 156 years of months is a small catalogue.
methods.test that would show it helps: Log score of the analog member versus climatology, walk forward from 1921 (so the catalogue has 50 years), and its marginal contribution to the BMA combination; expect weak but possibly positive skill at 12 months and none at 1 month.
methods.source_title: NOAA CPC: Constructed Analogue (CA) prediction of SST (van den Dool)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page says natural analogues are highly unlikely in high degree-of-freedom processes and builds CA by ridge regression applied to what followed; formulas correct.

methods.method: Forecast skill horizon by lead time
methods.what it does in its home field: Finds the lead time at which an ensemble stops beating a climatological distribution under a proper score; ECMWF found 16 to 23 days for instantaneous grid-point fields and longer for averaged fields.
methods.formula: D_h = mean log score skill of the h-month forecast versus climatology; h* = smallest h where the 90% bootstrap interval of D_h includes 0
methods.market analog: The engine's distribution forecasts of cumulative real return at horizons of 1, 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months.
methods.how the engine could use it: Compute D_h for each forecaster and the combination and report h*. Restrict tactical tilts to horizons below h* and treat forecasts beyond it as climatology; if the 12-month forecast has skill but the 1-month does not, sizing should change slowly rather than react monthly.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward since 1901: valuation forecasters should show D_h rising with horizon (averaged targets, like averaged weather fields, keep skill longer), while momentum shows skill only at short h. A turnover rule tied to h* should cut trading without lowering the log score.
methods.source_title: Buizza and Leutbecher, The forecast skill horizon (ECMWF Tech Memo 754)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Tech Memo 754 supports definition and 16 to 23 days, longer for averaged fields; h* rule is a reasonable operationalization.

methods.method: Reforecast training with a frozen model
methods.what it does in its home field: Reruns one frozen version of the current model over decades of past dates so post-processing has a long, consistent training set; calibrated forecasts from an older model with a reforecast beat a newer higher-resolution model without one.
methods.formula: for each past date t: forecast_t = M_frozen(data up to t); fit post-processing on {(forecast_t, outcome_t)} over the full archive
methods.market analog: The deployed version of the engine, rerun walk forward over every month since 1871 with data knowable at each date, produces the archive used to fit the EMOS, BMA and crash-probability recalibration layers.
methods.how the engine could use it: Version-stamp the engine and regenerate the full walk-forward archive whenever the model changes, so recalibration never mixes forecasts from different model versions. Record which version produced each live forecast so the evidence gate scores like with like.
methods.test that would show it helps: Fit the recalibration layer on a long reforecast archive versus a short trailing window of live forecasts; the long archive should give a better out-of-sample log score and a flatter PIT histogram, especially for crash months that a short window never contains.
methods.source_title: Hamill, Whitaker and Mullen, Reforecasts: an important dataset for improving weather predictions (BAMS 2006)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract supports frozen 1998 model reforecast and calibrated old model beating 2002 GFS; formula is a correct schematic.

methods.method: Weather roulette: log score as Kelly wealth
methods.what it does in its home field: A forecaster bets each period against a casino that prices outcomes from a reference forecast (in Palmer et al., a Gaussian centred on the high-resolution deterministic forecast with spread from its past errors), staking in proportion to its forecast probabilities and reinvesting; the EPS bettor turned 1 pound into more than 1030 pounds in a year betting on Heathrow temperature, and Roulston and Smith show ignorance equals the expected returns of such betting.
methods.formula: log(W_T / W_0) = sum_t [log f_t(b_t) - log c_t(b_t)], b_t the realized return bin, f the forecast and c the casino's reference probability (climatology in the engine's version)
methods.market analog: Bin monthly real returns (for example 20 equal-probability bins under climatology); the engine's mixture gives f_t for each bin.
methods.how the engine could use it: Report cumulative weather-roulette wealth of the engine versus climatology as a plain translation of log score skill into compounding, and use its drawdowns to show when the forecaster was losing to the baseline. This also links the log score directly to the Kelly and CRRA logic of the decision core.
methods.test that would show it helps: The wealth path should rise over 1901 to date with a growth rate equal to D (nats per month); periods of wealth drawdown longer than 10 years would flag regimes where the engine should revert to climatology.
methods.source_title: Palmer et al., Ensemble prediction: a pedagogical perspective (ECMWF Newsletter 106)
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: GBP 1030 and Roulston-Smith betting equivalence verified, but Palmer et al.'s casino sets odds from a Gaussian around the high-resolution deterministic forecast, not climatology.

methods.method: Data assimilation of the latent expected return
methods.what it does in its home field: Combines a model background with new observations, weighting each by its error covariance, to estimate the current state before each forecast; the ensemble Kalman filter estimates the background covariance from an ensemble.
methods.formula: mu_t|t = mu_t|t-1 + K_t (r_t - mu_t|t-1), K_t = P_t|t-1 / (P_t|t-1 + R); mu_t+1|t = alpha + phi mu_t|t, P_t+1|t = phi^2 P_t|t + Q
methods.market analog: The latent conditional expected real return is the state; realized monthly returns are very noisy observations (R large) and valuation variables shape the background through alpha and phi.
methods.how the engine could use it: Treat the forecaster's expected return as a background and assimilate each month's realized return with a small gain, so the engine updates beliefs gradually rather than refitting. Use the posterior variance P_t|t as an explicit parameter-uncertainty term added to the mixture variance.
methods.test that would show it helps: Compare the log score of forecasts using the assimilated mean and inflated variance against the raw forecaster, 1901 to date; the gain should be largest after regime breaks, and the PIT should be flatter because parameter uncertainty is no longer ignored.
methods.source_title: Evensen, Sequential data assimilation for nonlinear dynamics: the ensemble Kalman filter
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Evensen supports ensemble-estimated background covariance and observation weighting; scalar Kalman update and AR(1) predict step correct (posterior P_t|t = (1 - K_t) P_t|t-1 left implicit).

methods.method: Fellegi-Sunter probabilistic record linkage with a review band
methods.what it does in its home field: Decides whether two records (census, health, administrative) describe the same person or event from field-by-field agreement patterns, linking confident matches, rejecting confident non-matches and sending the ambiguous middle to clerical review at stated error rates.
methods.formula: weight = sum_k log(m_k / u_k) over agreeing fields + sum_k log((1 - m_k) / (1 - u_k)) over disagreeing fields; link if weight >= T_upper, non-link if weight <= T_lower, review otherwise
methods.market analog: Merging aliases, renamed firms, ticker changes, spin-offs and near-duplicate concepts so that every fact about one company or idea lands on one node.
methods.how the engine could use it: Run a Fellegi-Sunter pass over the 4,318 concepts and roughly 9,000 nodes (name, aliases, source domain, link neighbors as fields), auto-merge high-weight pairs, auto-separate low-weight pairs, and queue the middle band for the human desk, logging each review as a typed action.
methods.test that would show it helps: Hand-label 300 candidate pairs; compare precision and recall against exact-name matching at the same review budget; then check that merged nodes reduce contradictory facts per entity without raising false merges above 1%.
methods.source_title: Fellegi and Sunter, A Theory for Record Linkage, JASA 64 (1969)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page supports link / possible link / non-link at fixed error levels; log(m/u) agreement and log((1-m)/(1-u)) disagreement weights are correct.

methods.method: Link analysis of shared exposures
methods.what it does in its home field: In AML, fraud and investigative journalism, traverses networks of people, companies, accounts and addresses to find rings, common owners and hidden counterparties within a few degrees, as ICIJ did with the Panama Papers graph.
methods.formula: n/a
methods.market analog: Holdings that look diversified by ticker but share one supplier, customer, power source or funding channel, for example several AI names that all depend on one foundry or one hyperscaler's capex.
methods.how the engine could use it: Add typed supplier, customer, capex-dependency and financing links between the nine holdings and their key counterparties, then compute, for each pair of holdings, the count and weight of shared second-degree nodes as a concentration score feeding the expected-shortfall budget.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward from the earliest available supply-chain data: check whether pairs with more shared second-degree nodes show higher realized drawdown co-movement in the next 12 months than pairs with similar return correlation but fewer shared nodes.
methods.source_title: ICIJ, Wrangling 2.6TB of data: The people and the technology behind the Panama Papers (Apr 25, 2016)
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: ICIJ page supports graph traversal of people, companies and addresses (two degrees of separation); AML and fraud uses are not on the page; title is wrong.

methods.method: Isolation forest on the monthly market state
methods.what it does in its home field: Scores how easily a point can be separated from the rest by random axis-aligned splits; points isolated in few splits are anomalies. Used for fraud and network intrusion detection with linear time and no labels.
methods.market analog: Months whose combination of valuation, rates, inflation, momentum and volatility has little precedent, where any model fitted on history is extrapolating.
methods.how the engine could use it: Each month fit an isolation forest on the 14 state variables using only prior months, and use the anomaly score to widen forecast intervals or shrink the evidence gate's confidence when the current state is unusual.
methods.test that would show it helps: Walk forward since 1900: compare crash12, vol_next12 and absolute forecast error in the top anomaly-score decile against the rest; the method helps if forecast errors and crash rates are reliably higher there and if shrinking exposure in those months improves the 12% expected-shortfall hit rate.
methods.source_title: Liu, Ting and Zhou, Isolation Forest (ICDM 2008)
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: Formula correct as in paper (s, c(n), H(i) about ln(i)+0.5772); paper cites fraud and network intrusion but not equipment fault detection.

methods.method: Bayesian online changepoint detection
methods.what it does in its home field: Tracks, online, the posterior probability that the data-generating process changed at each past step by maintaining a distribution over run length; used in signal processing, robotics and monitoring.
methods.market analog: A volatility or correlation regime ending, such as the stock-bond correlation turning positive, before a rolling-window model notices.
methods.how the engine could use it: Run BOCPD on monthly real returns and on the 36-month stock-bond correlation with a prior hazard of 1/60 months; feed P(r_t = 0) into the regime models as an extra input and into the TLT hedge weight.
methods.test that would show it helps: Compare against the existing regime filter and a CUSUM test on detection lag for known breaks (1929, 1973, 2000, 2008, 2022) and on false alarms per decade; then check whether adding the changepoint probability lowers maxdd12 at equal ret12 in walk-forward runs.
methods.source_title: Adams and MacKay, Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (2007)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Recursion matches Algorithm 1 (with constant hazard H=1/lambda); paper lists process control, EEG, robotics and signal processing uses.

methods.method: Blend fast proxies with lagged ground truth and recalibrate
methods.what it does in its home field: In flu surveillance, combining Google Flu Trends with lagged CDC data and refitting the mapping over time substantially beat search data alone, which had overestimated for 100 of 108 weeks.
methods.formula: y_hat_t = a_t + b_t * proxy_t + c_t * y_{t-k}; coefficients refit each period on data available at t
methods.market analog: AI-buildout nowcasts from alternative data (job postings, web traffic, card panels, power interconnection queues) that proxy reported hyperscaler capex and revenue.
methods.how the engine could use it: For each alt-data nowcast, always include the last reported official value as a regressor and refit monthly in the walk-forward loop, and treat a nowcast without a lagged-truth anchor as inadmissible at the evidence gate.
methods.test that would show it helps: For each reported quarter, compare the mean absolute error of proxy-only, lagged-truth-only and blended nowcasts, fitted walk-forward; the blend should beat both, and its advantage should persist after the proxy's provider changes methodology.
methods.source_title: Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani, The Parable of Google Flu, Science 343 (2014)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper reports combining GFT with lagged CDC data and recalibration beats GFT or CDC alone (MAE 0.232 vs 0.486 and 0.311); 100 of 108 weeks confirmed; formula is a fair rendering.

methods.method: Ensemble spread as a forecast uncertainty signal
methods.what it does in its home field: ECMWF runs 51 forecasts from perturbed initial conditions and physics; the greater the spread across members, the greater the forecast uncertainty, and forecasters check that spread matches realized error.
methods.formula: spread_t = sd(member forecasts at t); skill check: corr(spread_t, |mean_forecast_t - outcome_t|) > 0, and mean spread about equal to RMSE of the ensemble mean
methods.market analog: Disagreement among the engine's regime models and forecasters about next-12-month return or crash risk.
methods.how the engine could use it: Record every forecaster's monthly output, compute their dispersion, and scale the expected-shortfall estimate or the CRRA sizing by spread when spread has shown skill.
methods.test that would show it helps: On walk-forward forecasts since 1900, regress absolute ret12 forecast error on lagged spread; then compare sizing with and without spread scaling on utility and ES breaches. Spread that is uncorrelated with error should be dropped.
methods.source_title: ECMWF, Medium-range forecasts documentation
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 51 perturbed members and 'greater the spread, greater the uncertainty' confirmed; the spread-error check is standard practice but not stated on this page. Formula is sound.

methods.method: Buhlmann credibility weighting of strategy records
methods.what it does in its home field: Actuaries set a policyholder's or class's rate as a blend of its own loss experience and the broader class mean, with weight Z = n/(n+K) rising with exposure and falling with process noise.
methods.formula: estimate = Z * Xbar + (1 - Z) * mu; Z = n / (n + K); K = EPV / VHM
methods.market analog: A strategy's backtested excess return is its own experience; the average realized performance of all strategies tried is the class mean.
methods.how the engine could use it: In the evidence gate, replace ad hoc discounts with credibility weights: estimate EPV from within-strategy monthly variance and VHM from the cross-section of strategy means, and shrink every strategy's record toward the class mean before sizing.
methods.test that would show it helps: Split history: estimate each tried strategy's mean on the first half, then compare the out-of-sample error of raw, credibility-weighted and fixed-haircut estimates on the second half. Credibility should cut squared error relative to the raw estimate.
methods.source_title: Curtis Gary Dean, Topics in Credibility Theory (SOA STAM-23-18)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dean's study note gives Z = n/(n+K), K = EPV/VHM and Z*Xbar + (1-Z)*mu exactly.

methods.method: Weight-of-evidence scorecard with an IV leakage alarm
methods.what it does in its home field: Credit scorers bin each variable, convert bins to weights of evidence, fit a logistic model and screen variables by information value; IV above about 0.5 is treated as suspicious for leakage.
methods.formula: WoE_i = ln(dist_good_i / dist_bad_i); IV = sum_i (dist_good_i - dist_bad_i) * WoE_i
methods.market analog: A crash12 classifier built from the 14 monthly state variables, where monotone, explainable bins matter more than a small accuracy gain.
methods.how the engine could use it: Build a walk-forward WoE scorecard for crash12 with bins fixed in advance (quintiles of each variable as of each month), report each variable's IV, and block any new feature whose IV exceeds 0.5 until a leakage audit passes.
methods.test that would show it helps: Compare walk-forward Brier score and AUC of the scorecard against logistic regression on raw variables and against the base rate; plant a deliberately leaked feature (next-month return) to confirm the IV alarm fires.
methods.source_title: scorecardmodel documentation: Weight of Evidence (WOE), In-Depth Guide
methods.checked: corrected by a second checker: WoE and IV formulas correct, but the R iv page has no 0.5 leakage threshold; the scorecardmodel WOE guide states '> 0.5 Suspicious, Investigate for data leakage'.

methods.method: Matrix factorization of the rule by month performance matrix
methods.what it does in its home field: Recommender systems factor a sparse user by item rating matrix into latent vectors with biases, predicting unseen ratings and revealing latent tastes.
methods.formula: r_hat_ui = mu + b_i + b_u + q_i' p_u; minimize sum (r_ui - r_hat_ui)^2 + lambda (||p_u||^2 + ||q_i||^2 + b_u^2 + b_i^2)
methods.market analog: Rules and signals play the role of users, months the role of items, and each cell is a rule's realized hit or excess return in that month; latent month factors are data-driven regimes.
methods.how the engine could use it: Fit a low-rank model (rank 3 to 5) on the rule by month matrix using only past months, read the month factors as candidate regimes, and predict a rule's next-month performance from the current month's factor estimate.
methods.test that would show it helps: Hold out random cells and the most recent months; compare RMSE against rule mean and month mean baselines, and check whether latent month factors predict ret12 better than the existing regime labels in walk-forward runs.
methods.source_title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky, Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems, IEEE Computer (Aug 2009)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Biased MF prediction and regularized objective match Eqs. 4 and 5 of Koren, Bell and Volinsky.

methods.method: Ladder-style leaderboard for strategy promotion
methods.what it does in its home field: Blum and Hardt's Ladder reports a new best holdout score only when a submission beats the current best by a set margin, which limits overfitting from repeated adaptive queries to one holdout.
methods.formula: n/a
methods.market analog: The engine repeatedly testing new rules against the same 156 years of monthly data, which is a reused holdout.
methods.how the engine could use it: Keep a single reserved holdout segment; let a new strategy replace the incumbent only if it beats it by a margin of at least one standard error of the holdout score, and count every query against the holdout in the evidence gate's trial tally.
methods.test that would show it helps: Simulate thousands of random rules with no true edge: compare the inflation of the best holdout score with free reuse versus the Ladder rule; then confirm that promoted real strategies degrade less on post-holdout data.
methods.source_title: Blum and Hardt, The Ladder: A Reliable Leaderboard for Machine Learning Competitions (arXiv 2015)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract supports limiting holdout overfitting; the paper's Figure 1 releases a new score only if it beats the previous best by more than eta.

methods.method: Pythagorean expectation applied to price versus fundamentals
methods.what it does in its home field: Sabermetricians estimate a team's true quality from runs scored and allowed; teams whose actual record beats their Pythagorean record tend to regress the next season because close-game luck does not persist.
methods.formula: W% = RS^c / (RS^c + RA^c), c about 1.82
methods.market analog: Price momentum that has run ahead of real earnings growth, the market's record outpacing its run differential.
methods.how the engine could use it: Define a gap equal to mom12_1 minus the log of one plus earn_g12, and treat large positive gaps as luck-heavy price gains that should mean-revert in the next 12 months.
methods.test that would show it helps: On Shiller data since 1871, compare ret12 and crash12 in months where mom12_1 > 0.15 and earn_g12 < 0 against all other months, walk forward; the analog helps only if the gap adds information beyond cape_pct and trend_gap.
methods.source_title: Steven J. Miller, A Derivation of the Pythagorean Won-Loss Formula in Baseball (arXiv 2005)
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Miller's abstract gives RS^c/(RS^c+RA^c) with best c about 1.82; the next-season regression claim is standard sabermetrics, not stated on this page.

methods.method: Ontology-backed digital twin to stress actions before taking them
methods.what it does in its home field: Palantir describes its Ontology as a digital twin of the organization: typed objects and links mirror real assets, and proposed actions are defined, parameterized and logged before they change anything.
methods.formula: n/a
methods.market analog: A twin of the model book (positions, exposures, hedges, links to suppliers and macro drivers) on which any proposed resize is simulated against historical and hypothetical scenarios.
methods.how the engine could use it: Make every OODA Act step an action type on the knowledge graph that first runs the proposal through the twin (analog months, stress scenarios, ES budget) and is blocked if the post-trade ES exceeds 12%.
methods.test that would show it helps: Replay past monthly decisions with and without the pre-check; count ES budget breaches avoided and the return given up, and verify that the twin's predicted scenario losses are calibrated against realized losses in matching historical windows.
methods.source_title: Palantir Foundry documentation: Ontology overview
methods.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Overview page calls the Ontology a digital twin of the organization with object, link and action types.

methods.method: Decision writeback and outcome scoring
methods.what it does in its home field: Palantir action types commit user decisions as transactions and capture them in an object type's writeback dataset, so the record of who decided what, with which inputs, stays joined to the data.
methods.formula: Brier = (1/N) * sum (p_i - o_i)^2 over logged probabilistic calls
methods.market analog: Each monthly sizing decision, its stated probabilities (crash12, bond_hedge12) and the evidence it cited, logged as a typed node linked to the outcome 12 months later.
methods.how the engine could use it: Write every desk decision and every rejected alternative back to the graph with the forecast probabilities used; after 12 months join outcomes and score both taken and not-taken calls, which also avoids the reject-inference bias of scoring only actions taken.
methods.test that would show it helps: After 24 logged months, compute Brier scores and reliability diagrams for logged calls versus the models' raw outputs; writeback helps if it exposes miscalibration that leads to a measurable Brier improvement in the following year.
